title: Churchill Refuses to Negotiate
text:
Winston Churchill became British prime minister on May 10, 1940, the day Germany attacked France and the Low Countries. Within two weeks the French front had collapsed and most of the British army was trapped at Dunkirk. It seemed possible that it would be lost entirely.

In the small War Cabinet, Foreign Secretary Lord Halifax argued that Britain should at least explore whether Mussolini's Italy might mediate terms with Hitler, while Britain still had something to bargain with. For several days, from May 25 to 28, the debate went back and forth. Churchill's position in his own party was not yet secure.

On the afternoon of May 28 Churchill met the wider group of ministers outside the War Cabinet and spoke to them frankly about the situation. According to the diary of Hugh Dalton, who was present, he told them that he had wondered whether it was his duty to consider negotiating, but had concluded that any terms would make Britain a slave state. He said that if this long island story of theirs was to end at last, let it end only when each of them lay choking in his own blood upon the ground.

The ministers cheered and crowded around him. Churchill reported their reaction to the War Cabinet, and the idea of negotiation was dropped.
lesson: In the darkest moment, a leader who states plainly what is at stake and what he will not give up can give doubters the courage to hold on.
people: Winston Churchill, Lord Halifax, Hugh Dalton
source: War Cabinet minutes, May 1940; Hugh Dalton's diary, May 28, 1940
